POSITIONS.md:136
- P-133 **The gap ledger's form.** A row's status cell holds exactly one word of seven: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`; no second status and nothing in brackets; a row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED` and its notes say which half is fixed (D1 of `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md` section 4.5). The rewrite of the ledger is split among many small workers, each with a slice of rows it can hold in context, never one worker over the whole ledger; the duplicate search is a separate step before it, whose groups tell the rewrite which rows to join. The class cell is `kind (area)`, the area one of parser, walk, checker, codegen, runtime, library, prelude, specification, tests, tools; a specification citation gives the file and the section, a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; a row is at most 1,200 characters, the open rows cut to it by the rewrite; the full earlier text of every changed row is in one history file, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md` (D2 to D5 at the proposal's defaults). The rows are sorted into topic sections, the rewrite's topical groups becoming the sections, each row keeping its number; a new row goes into the section its writer names, and row 83 becomes an eight-cell row in its section (D6). `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` owns the ledger's format and is the only way to write it (add with the template checked, note, close, duplicate, check); `facts-extract.sh` stays the one reader of every record, its ledger queries calling `ledger.py`'s parser. D7, numbering rows during parallel batches, is open.

POSITIONS.md:137
- P-134 **The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, and checked against what the workers did.** The skills distil the best practices found by every worker in this repository, for a reader new to it, which every agent is; he judges them with human eyes, and the coordinator helps him write them in the most concise and precise way. Agent shorthand stays where it serves; an internal reference that the record established is explained, since without FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX in context neither he nor an agent can follow it. The skill corrects the assumptions an agent brings from pre-training, so that it forms a correct model of Fortress as a language before it works on the repository that implements it: a "Fortress as a language" section stands in the opening of `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md`, which every agent reads, since nearly every agent writes a test program (`explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md`, `explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md` section D). Where a practice is in question, an archaeology worker checks what the batch workers actually did, as the search for their use of the `fortress` commands did, so that where a better way was found and agents still work around the issue, the skill states the better way. The register is about halfway toward ASD-STE100, Simplified Technical English: one instruction per sentence in the imperative, active voice, short sentences, the condition before the instruction, one word for one thing, no telegraphic or essayist shorthand, and no sentence that tells the reader neither what to do nor a fact needed to do it; without bloating the skills, whose token count matters, a rewrite never longer than what it replaces. Skill text follows ASD-STE100's split: a description of the concepts first, then short procedures, stated positively. He suspects the essayist register came into the skills from FACTS and POSITIONS, written in it by earlier models. Building happens in one area at a time (the interpreter, the compiled path, the library, the specification), which is why the parts are split by area; the skill says so in those terms. `SKILL.md` holds the concepts and the trigger to switch modes; the exploring procedure is a part loaded when the trigger fires. Knowledge that daily work needs stands in the part an agent loads when it needs it; a note stays named in a skill only with a trigger, when to open it, and a narrow way to read it. The record (FACTS, POSITIONS, the ledger, INDEX and the notes) is the project's memory, kept in the repository because a session can move to another container; `fortress-repo` defines it near its top, with its files, and the `coordinator` skill picks each worker's slice of it, so that the dependency runs one way and a worker never needs the `coordinator` skill. How a Claude Code session behaves (long commands, waits, interrupts, the permission check) belongs in `fortress-repo`, which every worker has loaded, not in a skill of its own; what only the coordinator needs of it goes to `coordinator`. The checker count and the distance are the ladder's metrics: the workflow's prompts say how to run them and the `coordinator` skill names them; `fortress-repo` holds nothing of them. `fortress-repo` carries no batch structure, on purpose: which roles exist, who builds, checks, runs the gate, commits and pushes to `main` are set by whoever writes the workflow or the brief, so that agents designing a workflow from the skill are not steered toward ours; the skill says how to do each thing, and the brief says which an agent does. The role split may later be written as behaviours a batch's instructions point to, in a skill of its own. An agent acts on its brief alone: the skill names no other authority over what it commits or pushes, and no rule an agent cannot act on (it cannot ask him). A worker works with three things, its brief, the record and the original tree, in one of two modes: building, where it stands on the record and carries out its mission, and exploring, where it has met something the record does not settle (a gap, two of the team's sources in conflict, new evidence against a decision), gathers evidence in the record first and then in the original tree, adds what it found to the record and returns to building. Where the team's sources disagree, the later one wins, the specification included. A worker never settles such a conflict itself, and never revises the specification to a later source on its own reading: the conflict is surfaced, and the curator rules after research by the nine steps; a decision on record is carried out, and questioned only on evidence the decision did not use. A conflict between the text and an implementation that no decision settles gets a ledger row and a test of the current behaviour; an `XXX` test belongs to repair work, where the current behaviour is tolerated for a time on purpose and the test is promoted once the fix is in. What a worker builds on while its question waits for him is left unsaid: it is case by case, and a reversible choice takes the path of least resistance without a rule. An agent takes the tree it starts from as green, starts with its own failing test, reuses only what its brief cites or its own work ran, and runs more only where its edit reaches; test first applies to an edit of source code. A point a brief wants reviewed is a "point to report", never a "stop", which reads as a condition that stops the worker. A skill's parts are written by the seven writing principles (`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`), which he has read and judged safe to apply to every rewrite: the writer applies them to a whole part at once, and he then reads it, not comment by comment. The earlier lenses note and the review-style profile are not a writer's brief. Before he reads a rewritten part, a cold reader given only the skill reads it as the workers who use it would, flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, the undefined terms and the gotchas; the coordinator reviews the findings, the writer fixes them with his comments so far, and only then does he read it. A comment on the review page marks a problem area, not a sentence to patch: the fix is made at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind. The skills are rewritten in place, git holding the earlier text. One writer does the writing, briefed by the coordinator, every comment fix on the page among its tasks, made from the coordinator's brief of his comment instead of the coordinator interpreting his words: it edits the skill files and commits them, and the coordinator keeps the review page in step, so that the writer's context holds only the writing. The writer is a headless Claude session (`explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`), since such a session keeps its prompt cache for an hour, as the coordinating session does, while an Agent-tool subagent keeps it for five minutes and so writes its whole context again when the curator's next comment comes later than that; the cache's one-hour writes cost more and are worth it. It is resumed for each writing task, and started fresh with only its standing brief when its history no longer serves, as after a large pass or the coordinator's compaction. Its standing order: ASD-STE100 at least halfway, terms defined first and then used, concise procedures, positive phrasing; and it does not take the register of what it reads, since FACTS, POSITIONS and many notes were written by earlier models in agent shorthand that the curator cannot follow cold, and the coordinator, which carries them in context, keeps drifting into it. A writer's minor decisions not taken are settled by the coordinator from the record, as his executive assistant, and not put to him; he is asked only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. A position's bold title here is the record's handle, not his words, and is never quoted to him as his. A glossary of terms, in a skill or on a page, is written as a dictionary is: each term and the noun phrase that opens its definition with no article ("revival", not "the revival").

POSITIONS.md:138
- P-135 **The coordinator rewrite's goals.** The `coordinator` skill is rewritten by a heavier process than `fortress-repo`'s, since the coordinator acts in several roles that work well and must not be lost to an ill-considered change. Its goals: one home for how the coordinator works, the protocol retired and its rules that bind workers moved to `fortress-repo`; every kind of record with one home and a stated purpose, the informal homes (the handover's first section, the held list, PLAN's old rule sections, the boot note's standing lines) retired or folded in, and the skill saying plainly what goes where; a lighter boot that keeps his awareness (the coordinator knows the project without him, never re-asks a decision, never sends a worker to measure again what is on record), the open question being FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX (their form, a grouping by topic, what they repeat of each other, what is always loaded and what is looked up), settled on evidence and a trial boot, not assumed; FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving workers' briefs; no role lost (executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst); the `fortress-repo` writing standard. The skill is tiered: a core always loaded, and sections loaded when the coordinator switches into a mode of work that is not needed all the time (running and reviewing a batch, process engineering, a post-mortem, among others), as the workers' skill separates building from exploring; the coordinator's modes are identified and described first. The batch workflow is in scope, since it is improved whenever it shows a problem. `cloud-container` follows by the `fortress-repo` method. The rewrite rests on the frontier model's own habits, not on a system designed around them: "I don't want a system of hundreds little rules with potentially contradicting dos and don'ts." The skill guides lightly, by a few general principles, among them how to talk to him in each situation, and the record is organized as the model organizes knowledge by itself: "Organization of the knowledge base should reflect the model's second nature, never fight it", which he names the rewrite's highest risk. So the natural baseline of the current models, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, is established before the design, and the design starts from what this project's environment adds to it: his review on a phone, dictation by speech to text, holding the open items of a long dictated message (preventing the wall-of-text spiral and recovering from it), and keeping a large body of project knowledge in order. The map also gives where each record home came from and which model made it. The map of the shape the rewrite starts from is `coordinator/process-engineering/coordinator-shape.md`. The skill is written from scratch by an Opus writer, from the sort of the rules against the baseline (what is kept, and the facts stated instead of rules), the map's problems to design against, and the writing principles; the writer does not read the existing skill, which is not refactored. A check against the sort's list after the draft shows whether anything kept was lost, and then the cold read follows as usual. A rule is kept when the failure it guards against is on record; the interview's self-report decides no drop, since the two disagree exactly on the rules that matter (the clock, closed decisions), and the interview showed only the record's default shape, a short current-state file with decisions and history apart, which is kept without instruction. The two sorts carry the map's handles, not the rule texts, and are not what he or the writer judges a rule by.

POSITIONS.md:139
- P-136 **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.

A finished agent's result is kept, an unfinished one runs from its start, and its worktree's leftovers are its starting point; a relaunch from the base restarts at the first stage instead. An `Agent`-tool worker continues from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's `agent()` calls in call order, so it needs the launch's arguments byte for byte and the same order of calls: a base given as a short hash where the launch gave the full hash misses the cache from the first call, and when cached stages resolve at once, a pipeline may call its next stage in another order than the live run did and miss from there. Where the call order would differ, the copy forces the live run's order, prompts unchanged, by wrapping `agent()` so that the finished calls are issued in the journal's order of their `started` lines. A copy that changes only what follows the cached prefix (a gate skipped, a commit's prompt extended) runs the changed call live and nothing before it. A stage stopped mid-work can leave its work in the tree. A commit stage killed before it had committed leaves its edits in the main tree, uncommitted, and a resume whose commit prompt names them (a changed prompt, so a new key) checks and keeps them and lands the batch. The cap's stops are not a crash, not memory and not a message; they fall while the curator is talking because the process runs continuously only while he or a check-in keeps it busy. 1	# Collaboration protocol
2	
3	How Pavol and Claude work together on the Fortress revival. Read at session
4	start, before anything else. It is six principles and a short list of hard
5	rules. The principles serve purposes, and the purposes govern: when a wording
6	and its purpose conflict, or when following a line would make things worse, do
7	the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix. Keep effort and
8	record in proportion: a side remark changes behaviour, not the record. Notice
9	what is going wrong, a file growing, a rule producing clutter, reports nobody
10	asked for, and propose the fix before Pavol has to point it out. His words
11	behind all of this are in `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`.
12	
13	## Hard rules
14	
15	These are not judgement calls.
16	
17	- Pavol decides what gets committed. A batch run waits for his yes, each
18	  time, and so does a Fable worker, except the design judgements principle 5
19	  lets the coordinator run on its own judgement. A stop a batch record reserves for him, a line of the
20	  model beyond the approved ones among them, does not hold a push or the next
21	  batch when it can be undone: it lands, and it is listed for his review. Standing approval covers only the approved ladder in
22	  `modernization-plan.md` and the push order below. A step his yes already
23	  covers is taken, not asked about again.
24	- Never committed: a model identifier (a model is named by its tier: Fable,
25	  Opus, Sonnet); a copyrighted PDF or deck, except an open-access paper whose license allows
26	  redistribution, committed beside its extract at his word, as the POPL 2019
27	  paper is, and the POPL 2019 talk's checked transcript with its slides' text,
28	  committed at his word (`research/decks/` is gitignored;
29	  cite by Wayback URL; `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries with brief
30	  attributed quotations); HANDOVER.md or ZIP contents without his go. His email
31	  is for attribution only.
32	- Every push: `git push origin main`, then
33	  `git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and
34	  `git push origin main:blinded-fable` (the branch the coordinating session was
35	  created from, which a rebuilt container clones); no other branch without
36	  permission (the transcript orphan branches excepted). Commit footer,
37	  exactly:
38	
39	  ```
40	  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
41	  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
42	  ```
43	
44	- A worker commits only the paths it wrote, as it goes, in one command
45	  (`git add -- <paths> && git commit -m … -- <paths>`), never a directory
46	  copy and never its scratch: probe programs, captured outputs, build logs,
47	  lists and copies of tools stay under the worktree's `tmp/`, which is
48	  ignored, and it pushes only after `git log origin/main..main` shows nothing
49	  but its own commits; the coordinator reviews after and fixes by a further
50	  commit. A staged change of more than a few hundred lines is read with
51	  `git diff --cached --stat` before it is committed.
52	- The gate: on a clean build, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` with zero
53	  failures, the four-thread `atomic` runs, the ladder regression; the checker
54	  count reported, never red on its own. Every edit under the original tree is
55	  test first: the test written and seen failing through the harness before
56	  the fix, then seen passing after it, and kept in the corpus; the test and
57	  the fix may land in one commit, and the edit is flagged at commit. The
58	  skeptic reads that order from the worker's transcript and runs no build to
59	  repeat it. Nothing is committed to show it but the test and the report's
60	  quoted lines.
61	- Never the AskUserQuestion dialog; options go in plain text.
62	
63	## Principles
64	
65	**1. We are custodians of their language, not its authors.** Finish what the
66	designers intended, judged by the specification and the library's own practice;
67	where they conflict, the type group's later, implementation-informed word weighs
68	more. So: no self-credit anywhere committed, attribution reconstructed where git
69	does not record it, provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports
70	rather than source comments, every claim verified against a primary source. The
71	notation is what the project exists for; a change to a line of the model is shown
72	to him as a diff.
73	
74	**2. A design question is answered from the evidence before it reaches him.**
75	What the mathematics says; what each path does today, measured; what the
76	specification says under every spelling; what the library already does in the
77	same family and where the designers departed from Java; what the peers do; what
78	the commits say; then the derivation from his principles and the decision in
79	his words. Solutions are the language's and the library's, not the first two
80	someone wrote down: a brief states the problem and never the expected answer, a
81	worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language offers before a
82	fork reaches him, and a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the
83	library gets around it. When something goes wrong or is undecided, the answer
84	is a deeper pass, never a halt, a rollback or a bisection of a merged batch.
85	One variable per step; reproduce before explaining; a timing names the machine
86	it ran on (`nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK,
87	`FORTRESS_THREADS`), and only a pair taken in one run measures a difference.
88	A timing of the interpreter is not taken or recorded, since no decision rests
89	on it (POSITIONS 2026-09-19).
90	
91	**3. He carries the responsibility, so his attention is the scarcest thing we
92	spend.** He reads on a phone, often one earlier turn at a time. One ask per
93	message, in this order: the question in one line; the context in short bullets,
94	in principle 2's order, with a refresher first where the subject is new to him
95	(why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it); the options,
96	numbered, each with what it does, what it touches and what it costs; what a yes
97	commits him to and what a no costs; the recommendation, one line, last and never
98	instead of the explanation (`coordinator/answer-form-archaeology.md`). Where we
99	think he is wrong, we say so and show why. Decisions one at a time, each with a
100	default he can accept without the argument; the argument goes in the review. A
101	document for his approval is published as a rendered page and he gets its link,
102	not a diff. Plain short sentences and short paragraphs, lists not tables,
103	numbers as K or M, a new term defined where it is used; explain it, don't just
104	name it. Say what you mean: where a literal phrase exists, use it; no metaphor
105	or turn of phrase in place of a direct statement. When he is reading and
106	replying turn by turn, restate and hold: each point in a line of our own words
107	on the held list, the reply only acknowledges each new point in a line and says
108	"holding", three lines at most, never the whole list again, nothing argued until
109	he says he is done, and no point is answered by being on the list; a point he
110	marks "now" is not held. A decision made inside a worker's report is not made
111	until he has seen it. Time is read from the clock, never guessed. While a batch
112	runs he hears nothing unless something is wrong, and never about the harness's
113	reminders or our record edits. A result reaches him only as a turn's final text.
114	
115	**4. Keep the project on track for him.** Every open issue is held in the order
116	it needs deciding (`PLAN.md`) and brought to him one at a time; nothing he must
117	decide is held only in the coordinator's context. A fork a probe can settle is
118	probed before the batch is briefed. Closed decisions are not revisited and
119	settled questions are not re-asked: losing an order to compaction and asking
120	again is the same failure as inventing one. The same holds for method: before a
121	thing is done a new way, the record is searched for how it was done last time.
122	Idle time goes to parked research; a new deliverable is discussed before it is
123	made; what needs his machine is parked, not simulated. When a goal is unclear,
124	ask, and when we act on one reading of it, say which.
125	
126	**5. The coordinator's context is the project's memory; spend it on
127	judgement.** Delegate by default: exploration, tracing, surveys and big
128	searches go to a worker that returns a summary, and work with no dependency on
129	what is running starts at once. Boot reads the record and nothing else, no
130	directory listings, every command's output bounded. Workers run on Opus,
131	Sonnet for archaeology. A Fable judgement runs without asking, sparingly, for a
132	design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and
133	the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file
134	and the record has been searched and does not settle it; he learns of it when
135	it is put to him in the ask form. Any other Fable worker waits for his yes: a
136	question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice,
137	one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants
138	Fable and Opus working apart (`coordinator/fable-use-archaeology.md`). A decision that
139	touches two of the specification, the interpreter and the compiler is made in
140	two steps, cheaper workers gathering cited evidence and the judgement at the
141	top tier. A brief names its reader and its question, and points at the earlier
142	research and documents on file instead of restating them, so that nothing on
143	record is rediscovered. What the record has measured the brief hands over as
144	findings to cite, with their sources, never as claims to verify by running them
145	again; it names the one thing that is new to measure and asks only for that. A
146	finding is measured again only when the tree has changed under it since, and
147	the brief says what changed. The clean worker of principle 2, on a design fork,
148	is kept clean of our options, not of our measurements: it reads its question
149	first, and measures only where no record answers it.
150	
151	**6. The record describes the present, each thing written once, so that a
152	resumed coordinator knows the project without him.** A fact in FACTS with its
153	source and its test, in a few lines with the detail left in the report it
154	cites, and with no date; a position in
155	POSITIONS as it stands, under its title, his words only where they are the
156	position; the provenance of both in the history files; what is in flight in
157	the boot note, rewritten whole. A wrong line is
158	fixed, not footnoted; a side remark changes behaviour, not the record; a
159	one-off go is written nowhere. The rest is `coordinator/README.md`.
160	
161	## What keeps going wrong
162	
163	Named so that the next boot sees it: walls of text and the clever register;
164	time guessed, not read; a fork put to him before the library's own way was
165	checked; standing orders and techniques invented when the record held one, or
166	lost and re-asked; corrections appended instead of fixed, and one remark of his
167	written into several files; a rule followed to the letter where that made
168	clutter; a brief that told a worker to "verify, do not trust" the record and to
169	measure every way on both paths, so that it re-ran measurements already on file; a rule of
170	the batch workflow applied where its purpose did not hold, so that a finished

176

and its purpose conflict, or when following a line would make things worse, do
the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix. Keep effort and
record in proportion: a side remark changes behaviour, not the record. Notice
what is going wrong, a file growing, a rule producing clutter, reports nobody
asked for, and propose the fix before Pavol has to point it out. His words
behind all of this are in `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`.

## Hard rules

These are not judgement calls.

- Pavol decides what gets committed. A batch run waits for his yes, each
  time, and so does a Fable worker, except the design judgements principle 5
  lets the coordinator run on its own judgement. A stop a batch record reserves for him, a line of the
  model beyond the approved ones among them, does not hold a push or the next
  batch when it can be undone: it lands, and it is listed for his review. Standing approval covers only the approved ladder in
  `modernization-plan.md` and the push order below. A step his yes already
  covers is taken, not asked about again.
- Never committed: a model identifier (a model is named by its tier: Fable,
  Opus, Sonnet); a copyrighted PDF or deck, except an open-access paper whose license allows
  redistribution, committed beside its extract at his word, as the POPL 2019
  paper is, and the POPL 2019 talk's checked transcript with its slides' text,
  committed at his word (`research/decks/` is gitignored;
  cite by Wayback URL; `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries with brief
  attributed quotations); HANDOVER.md or ZIP contents without his go. His email
  is for attribution only.
- Every push: `git push origin main`, then
  `git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and
  `git push origin main:blinded-fable` (the branch the coordinating session was
  created from, which a rebuilt container clones); no other branch without
  permission (the transcript orphan branches excepted). Commit footer,
  exactly:

  ```
  Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
  Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
  ```

- A worker commits only the paths it wrote, as it goes, in one command
  (`git add -- <paths> && git commit -m … -- <paths>`), never a directory
  copy and never its scratch: probe programs, captured outputs, build logs,
  lists and copies of tools stay under the worktree's `tmp/`, which is
  ignored, and it pushes only after `git log origin/main..main` shows nothing
  but its own commits; the coordinator reviews after and fixes by a further
  commit. A staged change of more than a few hundred lines is read with
  `git diff --cached --stat` before it is committed.
- The gate: on a clean build, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` with zero
  failures, the four-thread `atomic` runs, the ladder regression; the checker
  count reported, never red on its own. Every edit under the original tree is
  test first: the test written and seen failing through the harness before
  the fix, then seen passing after it, and kept in the corpus; the test and
  the fix may land in one commit, and the edit is flagged at commit. The
  skeptic reads that order from the worker's transcript and runs no build to
  repeat it. Nothing is committed to show it but the test and the report's
  quoted lines.
- Never the AskUserQuestion dialog; options go in plain text.

## Principles

**1. We are custodians of their language, not its authors.** Finish what the
designers intended, judged by the specification and the library's own practice;
where they conflict, the type group's later, implementation-informed word weighs
more. So: no self-credit anywhere committed, attribution reconstructed where git
does not record it, provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports
rather than source comments, every claim verified against a primary source. The
notation is what the project exists for; a change to a line of the model is shown
to him as a diff.

**2. A design question is answered from the evidence before it reaches him.**
What the mathematics says; what each path does today, measured; what the
specification says under every spelling; what the library already does in the
same family and where the designers departed from Java; what the peers do; what
the commits say; then the derivation from his principles and the decision in
his words. Solutions are the language's and the library's, not the first two
someone wrote down: a brief states the problem and never the expected answer, a
worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language offers before a
fork reaches him, and a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the
library gets around it. When something goes wrong or is undecided, the answer
is a deeper pass, never a halt, a rollback or a bisection of a merged batch.
One variable per step; reproduce before explaining; a timing names the machine
it ran on (`nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK,
`FORTRESS_THREADS`), and only a pair taken in one run measures a difference.
A timing of the interpreter is not taken or recorded, since no decision rests
on it (POSITIONS 2026-09-19).

**3. He carries the responsibility, so his attention is the scarcest thing we
spend.** He reads on a phone, often one earlier turn at a time. One ask per
message, in this order: the question in one line; the context in short bullets,
in principle 2's order, with a refresher first where the subject is new to him
(why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it); the options,
numbered, each with what it does, what it touches and what it costs; what a yes
commits him to and what a no costs; the recommendation, one line, last and never
instead of the explanation (`coordinator/answer-form-archaeology.md`). Where we
think he is wrong, we say so and show why. Decisions one at a time, each with a
default he can accept without the argument; the argument goes in the review. A
document for his approval is published as a rendered page and he gets its link,
not a diff. Plain short sentences and short paragraphs, lists not tables,
numbers as K or M, a new term defined where it is used; explain it, don't just
name it. Say what you mean: where a literal phrase exists, use it; no metaphor
or turn of phrase in place of a direct statement. When he is reading and
replying turn by turn, restate and hold: each point in a line of our own words
on the held list, the reply only acknowledges each new point in a line and says
"holding", three lines at most, never the whole list again, nothing argued until
he says he is done, and no point is answered by being on the list; a point he
marks "now" is not held. A decision made inside a worker's report is not made
until he has seen it. Time is read from the clock, never guessed. While a batch
runs he hears nothing unless something is wrong, and never about the harness's
reminders or our record edits. A result reaches him only as a turn's final text.

**4. Keep the project on track for him.** Every open issue is held in the order
it needs deciding (`PLAN.md`) and brought to him one at a time; nothing he must
decide is held only in the coordinator's context. A fork a probe can settle is
probed before the batch is briefed. Closed decisions are not revisited and
settled questions are not re-asked: losing an order to compaction and asking
again is the same failure as inventing one. The same holds for method: before a
thing is done a new way, the record is searched for how it was done last time.
Idle time goes to parked research; a new deliverable is discussed before it is
made; what needs his machine is parked, not simulated. When a goal is unclear,
ask, and when we act on one reading of it, say which.

**5. The coordinator's context is the project's memory; spend it on
judgement.** Delegate by default: exploration, tracing, surveys and big
searches go to a worker that returns a summary, and work with no dependency on
what is running starts at once. Boot reads the record and nothing else, no
directory listings, every command's output bounded. Workers run on Opus,
Sonnet for archaeology. A Fable judgement runs without asking, sparingly, for a
design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and
the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file
and the record has been searched and does not settle it; he learns of it when
it is put to him in the ask form. Any other Fable worker waits for his yes: a
question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice,
one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants
Fable and Opus working apart (`coordinator/fable-use-archaeology.md`). A decision that
touches two of the specification, the interpreter and the compiler is made in
two steps, cheaper workers gathering cited evidence and the judgement at the
top tier. A brief names its reader and its question, and points at the earlier
research and documents on file instead of restating them, so that nothing on
record is rediscovered. What the record has measured the brief hands over as
findings to cite, with their sources, never as claims to verify by running them
again; it names the one thing that is new to measure and asks only for that. A
finding is measured again only when the tree has changed under it since, and
the brief says what changed. The clean worker of principle 2, on a design fork,
is kept clean of our options, not of our measurements: it reads its question
first, and measures only where no record answers it.

**6. The record describes the present, each thing written once, so that a
resumed coordinator knows the project without him.** A fact in FACTS with its
source and its test, in a few lines with the detail left in the report it
cites, and with no date; a position in
POSITIONS as it stands, under its title, his words only where they are the
position; the provenance of both in the history files; what is in flight in
the boot note, rewritten whole. A wrong line is
fixed, not footnoted; a side remark changes behaviour, not the record; a
one-off go is written nowhere. The rest is `coordinator/README.md`.

## What keeps going wrong

Named so that the next boot sees it: walls of text and the clever register;
time guessed, not read; a fork put to him before the library's own way was
checked; standing orders and techniques invented when the record held one, or
lost and re-asked; corrections appended instead of fixed, and one remark of his
written into several files; a rule followed to the letter where that made
clutter; a brief that told a worker to "verify, do not trust" the record and to
measure every way on both paths, so that it re-ran measurements already on file; a rule of
the batch workflow applied where its purpose did not hold, so that a finished
batch waited on a whole gate rerun for a repair that only added tests, or on
owed tests a later batch could write (POSITIONS 2026-09-29): a rule is weighed
by what it costs against what it protects. Scratch committed as evidence, and
long runs awaited by agents with large contexts, so that a batch paid more to
record and to wait than to change Fortress (post-mortem 2026-09-29).

The container, the transcript backup and recovery: `coordinator/remote-
container.md`. The batch workflow's stages, stops and tiers:
`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`.

## 1. The goals, as reflected and corrected

From this session on 2026-10-10 and the boot note (`held-list.md` line 7):

1. One home for how the coordinator works. The protocol is retired. Its rules that bind workers move to the `fortress-repo` skill.
2. The `coordinator` skill probably loaded whole, because the roles interleave. Pavol leans this way and wants the facts first.
3. A lighter boot that keeps the awareness he relies on: the coordinator knows the project without him re-explaining it, never re-asks his decisions, and never sends workers to re-measure what is on record. The open question is FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX: their form (the optimized build still carries debug content), consolidation by topic, the duplication between FACTS and POSITIONS, and what is always loaded against what is looked up, a cheap worker that holds the text and answers questions among the options.
4. FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX keep serving workers' briefs.
5. No role is lost: executive assistant, batch coordinator, roadmap architect, briefer of workers, analyst.
6. The `fortress-repo` writing standard (`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`; POSITIONS, "The skills are written for a reader new to the repository ...").
7. `cloud-container` rewritten by the `fortress-repo` method.

Not a goal: no fact or decision changes its content, only its form and its home. (The draft also excluded the batch workflow; the curator corrected that on the page: the workflow is improved whenever it shows a problem, and running and reviewing a batch is one of the coordinator's modes.)

## 2. The boot today

The boot reads eight things. Sizes are bytes on `main`; tokens use the record's own ratios: 2.5 bytes a token for FACTS, 2.7 for INDEX, 3.0 for prose.

- `CLAUDE.md`: 1.8K bytes, about 0.6K tokens.
- `explorations/protocol.md`: 11.6K bytes, about 3.9K tokens.
- `explorations/coordinator/README.md`: 4.9K bytes, about 1.6K tokens.
- `FACTS.md`: 300K bytes, about 120K tokens.
- `POSITIONS.md`: 98K bytes, about 33K tokens.
- `INDEX.md`: 182K bytes, about 67K tokens.
- The handover's first section (`explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`, lines 1 to 68): 41K bytes, about 14K tokens.
- The boot note (`held-list.md` line 7): 8.8K bytes, about 2.9K tokens.

Together: 649K bytes, about 243K tokens of record. With the fixed part of a session (system prompt, tools, skills, about 56K) and the compaction summary (about 18K), a boot reaches about 317K. Pavol's figure of 300K after a restart matches.

The boot grew by half in two weeks. On 2026-09-27 the same files were 422K bytes (that note estimated about 125K tokens, with rougher ratios); now they are 649K. FACTS went from 155K to 300K bytes and INDEX from 83K to 182K. FACTS was cut by 92K on 10-02 and has grown again since. The consolidations before batches 12 and 13 changed it by +2.2K and +0.2K: they did not shrink it.

If the skill's `boot.md` is followed rather than the README, the held list below the boot note is read too: 26K bytes, about 9K tokens more.

**Sources.** `wc -c` on each file at `fb1aa7c7b`; the handover's first section is lines 1 to 68 (its next heading is line 69). ## 3. The map, by kind of content

Seven kinds. For each: where it lives, who reads it, when, its size, and where it repeats.

Readers: **boot** is the coordinator at every boot; **on demand** is the coordinator when a task calls for it; **briefs** are workers through the slice of the record a brief gives them (`facts-extract.sh` queries, the batch briefing); **skill** is workers through a skill they load.

Boot.

123	### What an entry is
124	
125	**Its purpose.** An entry lets a worker or the coordinator act right without opening the report, and tells it when the report is needed. FACTS does this for what is true of the tree. POSITIONS does it for what the curator decided, so that no one acts against a decision or asks him again.
126	
127	**A FACTS entry** holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact in one sentence: the fact as it stands now; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks, what avoids it, or which row or decision it bears on; the test that gates it, or its source when no test does; the number of the decision it builds, if any; and the report section that holds the detail.
128	
129	**A POSITIONS entry** holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; what the decision means for the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. The FACTS entries that build a decision give its number, and the decision does not list them.
130	
131	**The questions.** Picture the reader: a worker new to the repository who gets the entry in a brief and acts on it alone, or the coordinator who chooses the next work. Write as for a capable colleague who takes over tomorrow and cannot ask you. Ask of each sentence:
132	
133	1. Without it, would the reader do something else: choose another test, row, file or way, or decide otherwise? Keep it. F-53: an edit can move 2 to 4 errors that it does not touch, so a move that small does not show its effect.
134	2. Without it, would the reader misread another sentence? Keep it. F-58 says that the five powers fail because two declarations of `^` tie. Without that, a reader takes them for numeral work.
135	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, what it replaced, what was corrected, "no longer"? It goes to the history.
136	4. Is it detail that the reader needs only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing, a mechanism? It stays in the report, and the entry names the section.
137	5. Does another entry or a skill say it already? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
138	6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count. Say in a few words what a code stands for (decision D, E3).
139	
140	Questions 3 to 5 move a sentence; they do not lose it. Four habits put in an entry what belongs elsewhere: the lab notebook (how it was found), the changelog (what changed), the citation reflex (a line number on each claim) and the cache (a copy of another entry). One habit cuts too much: bare numbers and codes. "With the diff it has 14" tells nothing until it says 14 of what.

142	**A count that each landing changes**, such as the distance to the switch-over, has one entry: the current value, what it counts, the kinds that lead, and how to read a move. ## Part 2: the record-keeping part of the `coordinator` skill, a draft

This is a draft of the record-keeping part of the `coordinator` skill: the form of a FACTS or POSITIONS entry, and the pass by which the coordinator turns what a worker wrote into entries. It would replace "How the records are kept" in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/roles-and-records.md`. The `fortress-repo` skill keeps how workers read and use the record, and how they edit it when a brief asks them to; the last two sections list what changes there and in the other places that state the structure today. It opens with "What an entry is", the definition that the writers of the consolidation get, written to be quoted whole in a brief, and five worked examples; neither marks its sentences. Below them, each sentence is marked (his words), (on record) or (new). "His words" includes the framing he gave through the coordinator on 2026-10-13, about 09:20 UTC, and his chat messages and page comments of that day, quoted with their UTC times. Part 5 lists where each point of the test and of his comments went.

"What an entry is" replaces the nine principles of the earlier draft, which he commented on from 15:25 to 16:03 UTC; principles 1 to 6 are in it. Principles 7, 8 and 9 were about how the coordinator works, not about how an entry is written, so they are out: their items belong to other parts of the `coordinator` skill (`process-engineering/coordinator-skill-outline.md`), items 33 and 35 to 37 to Core 5 and Part 6, items 38 to 42 to Core 5 and `fortress-repo`, item 34 to Part 1, and item 31 to Core 2.

### What an entry is

**Its purpose.** An entry lets a worker or the coordinator act right without opening the report, and tells it when the report is needed. FACTS does this for what is true of the tree. POSITIONS does it for what the curator decided, so that no one acts against a decision or asks him again.

**A FACTS entry** holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact in one sentence: the fact as it stands now; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks, what avoids it, or which row or decision it bears on; the test that gates it, or its source when no test does; the number of the decision it builds, if any; and the report section that holds the detail.

**A POSITIONS entry** holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; what the decision means for the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. The FACTS entries that build a decision give its number, and the decision does not list them.

**The questions.** Picture the reader: a worker new to the repository who gets the entry in a brief and acts on it alone, or the coordinator who chooses the next work. Write as for a capable colleague who takes over tomorrow and cannot ask you. Ask of each sentence:

1. Without it, would the reader do something else: choose another test, row, file or way, or decide otherwise? Keep it. F-53: an edit can move 2 to 4 errors that it does not touch, so a move that small does not show its effect.
2. Without it, would the reader misread another sentence? Keep it. F-58 says that the five powers fail because two declarations of `^` tie. Without that, a reader takes them for numeral work.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, what it replaced, what was corrected, "no longer"? It goes to the history.
4. Is it detail that the reader needs only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing, a mechanism? It stays in the report, and the entry names the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it already? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count. Say in a few words what a code stands for (decision D, E3).

Questions 3 to 5 move a sentence; they do not lose it. Four habits put in an entry what belongs elsewhere: the lab notebook (how it was found), the changelog (what changed), the citation reflex (a line number on each claim) and the cache (a copy of another entry). One habit cuts too much: bare numbers and codes. "With the diff it has 14" tells nothing until it says 14 of what.

**A count that each landing changes**, such as the distance to the switch-over, has one entry: the current value, what it counts, the kinds that lead, and how to read a move. The batch's commit stage rewrites the value at each landing. Other entries give that entry's number, not the value. The counts by kind stay in the file that the gate writes. A count from one measurement is not kept current: its entry says so, and keeps the parts that a decision reads.

**The size.** About 240 entries stay, and the goal of about 145K characters for both files allows about 600 each. So 600 is a check, not a cap. An entry may pass it when the questions keep a sentence that needs the room. Its writer names, in the chunk's report, the decision or the misreading that the sentence prevents, and shorter entries pay for it: a chunk's total stays under 600 characters times its entries. The record test checks the result: no worse than 27 of 30.

**The register** is halfway to ASD-STE100: one statement per sentence, active voice, short sentences, one word for one thing. Use no shorthand that a reader new to the project cannot follow. Say what every number counts.

**The curator's words.** Condense what he said into the position, in this register, and keep the part of his rule that cuts. Quote him only where the exact words are the decision, as in the goal "the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability". His words as he dictated them go to the history, with their time.

POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`). Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the
record file and its history together.

  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:

  Each write needs --from or --note.

      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`. Each may be followed by one indented

`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a pointer to no live entry, or quoted words that do not open the
target's title; with --base, an entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now

- `merge` and `remove` are commands because pointers must follow: `merge` rewrites every `F-n` to `F-m`, and `remove` refuses while a pointer to the entry remains. That is integrity, not provenance.
- Commit messages do not cite FACTS entries; reports and tests cite entries and rows, and commits cite rows. Nothing changes there. The history is not for tracing a code change: `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry once the numbers are in.
- What the history adds over git, honestly: the reason and the source per entry, which a commit message gives per commit over dozens of entries; the earlier line beside that reason in one read, with no git and in a shallow clone; and the identity of an entry through a merge. The earlier line costs the writer nothing, since the tool copies it. What the writer must give is `--from` or `--note`, the one thing git cannot give per entry. So the history is worth keeping at exactly that price and no more.

## 3. The design as it should be built

For the builder's brief. Each item ends with its status against the design: as designed, changed, or new.

**The entry.**

- One line: `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in `FACTS.md`, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in `POSITIONS.md`. A number is never reused or changed. The title and the text are rewritten freely. (as designed)
- The tool refuses an entry with a line break. (new)
- A pointer is the target's number in the sentence that needs it: `It builds P-48.` Words beside it are the writer's and are not checked. The tool checks only that the number resolves to a live entry. No refresh of other entries' lines on a retitle. (changed: 3.1.2 and decision 4)
- A link is written once, in the entry whose sentence needs it. No "Built:" lists; `P-48+` lists the entries that build a position. (as designed)
- The detail's home is the report's path and a heading in quotes, resolved as `doc:` resolves one. (as designed)

**The history.**

- The files stay `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`. The numbering commit rewrites each from scratch: a header that names the commit holding the old file, then one `numbered` block per entry. Nothing is frozen and no hash is kept. (changed: 3.2.1)
- A block is the ledger's: `### F-87`, a blank line, one provenance line, a blank line, the earlier line verbatim. The provenance line, in this order: the UTC time from the clock, the kind, `from` each report section, `commit` the hash, `by` who, then the note after a colon. The `numbered` block has no earlier line; its note gives the line at the base and the former titles, each in quotes. (as designed in form; the `numbered` block's content changed)
- The kinds are derived by the tool: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved`, `merged into F-n`, `removed`, `numbered`. No `title was`. (changed: 3.2.3)
- The block keeps the earlier line. (as designed, decision 2)
- A POSITIONS change's `--note` holds his words with their UTC time where they are the reason. (as designed)

**The write.** `record.py` beside `ledger.py`, importing its lock, its one-step write and its word matching. Its commands:

- `add F|P --section TITLE FILE PROVENANCE`: the highest number ever used plus one, at the end of the section. (as designed)
- `set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] PROVENANCE`: the whole new line, with or without its number; the tool derives the kind. (as designed, the kind now derived)
- `merge N --into M FILE PROVENANCE`: removes N, rewrites M, rewrites every `F-N` pointer to `F-M`, one block each. (as designed)
- `remove N PROVENANCE`: refuses while a pointer to N remains, naming each. (as designed)
- `apply FILE PROVENANCE`: many changes from one file, checked against the resulting state, then written under one lock, or none. A new entry is written as `F-?1`, `F-?2` and so on, under its `## Section` heading, and the placeholder is replaced by the number everywhere in the file at apply, as the gather replaces `NEW-<rung>-<n>` for ledger rows (`climb-batch-workflow.md:160`). Each entry line may be followed by one indented line, its own provenance: `  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; note: WHY`. (as designed; the check against the resulting state and the placeholders are new)
- Provenance options: `--from PATH#HEADING` (repeatable; refused unless exactly one heading of the file holds it), `--commit HASH` (refused unless in `HEAD`'s history), `--by WHO`, `--note WHY`. A write with neither `--from` nor `--note` is refused. (as designed)
- Refused only for what breaks the store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve, no provenance, a line break. Never for size. (as designed)
- The lock file beside the record; the history appended first; the file replaced in one step. The tool does not commit. (as designed)
- The section parser reads `## ` and `### ` headings; an entry's section is the nearest heading above it of either level. (new)

**The read.** In `facts-extract.sh`:

- `F-87`, `P-48`: the entry. (as designed)
- `F-87+`: the entry, the entries it points to and the entries that point to it, each once, one level. (as designed)
- `history:F-87`: the entry's blocks, oldest first. Nothing else: the linked entries are `F-87+`, and the report sections are a scout's `doc:` read. (changed: replaces `trace:`)
- A title query that matches no current title searches the former titles in the history and prints the entry with one line saying it was retitled. (as designed)
- `title_of` skips the number, in the numbering commit. (new)
- Not built: `history-find:`. The old texts are in git, and `grep` over `git show HASH:FILE` finds them. (changed)

**The checks.** `record.py check [--base COMMIT]`. The first four fail; the rest are reported.

1. Every entry is one line of the form `- F-n **...**`; no number is on two lines.
2. Every number in a file has a `numbered` or `added` block, and every number in a history is in its file or its last block is `merged into` or `removed`.
3. Every `F-n` and `P-n` in either file resolves to a live entry.
4. With `--base`: every entry at COMMIT is its line now, or its line at COMMIT is the earlier line of a block in its history.
5. Reported: every `--from` path and every report section an entry cites resolves; the entries over 600 characters, with their sizes.

(as designed for 1 to 5 and 7 to 8; the quoted-words rule of 4, the frozen-part hash of 6 and `--outside` of 9 are dropped: changed)

**The numbering.** One commit by a script, `tools/record-number.py`, before the consolidation moves any line.

- Each entry's number is its line at the base: FACTS lines 7 to 219, POSITIONS 7 to 145. The unused numbers stay unused. (as designed)
- The script rewrites both history files as above, with the former titles matched by exact title and by a shared opening of 60 characters. (changed: 3.6.3)
- It converts the pointers by title inside the record to numbers where one entry matches (about 83 inside FACTS, 67 from FACTS to POSITIONS, 21 the other way), and lists the ambiguous ones. It does the same in `PLAN.md`, `review-queue.md`, `climb-batch-workflow.md`, `BOOT.md`, `HELD.md` and the kit's `key.md`, keeping the quoted words after the number. (as designed)
- It changes `fill.py` to resolve `{FACTS n}` by the number. (new)
- It checks that each entry is its line at the base with the number added and nothing else changed, that every title citation in a tracked file that resolved before resolves to the same entry after, and that `record.py check` passes. `check-verbatim.py` is retired after it. (as designed)
- The dated notes and the three `sources.md` files are not edited. (as designed)

**The tests.** `tools/test_record.py`, over a temporary copy of the record, as `test_ledger.py` does: one test per command, the refusals, `apply` all-or-none with a placeholder, `check --base` catching a hand edit, the title fallback, a `###` section. (as designed, the list new)

**The cost.** About 450 lines for `record.py`, 80 in `facts-extract.py`, 200 for the tests, 200 for the numbering script. One Opus worker, about 0.8M tokens written; it stops and reports at 1.2M. The record test's estimate ran 56 percent over (2.49M against 1.6M), so the stop is the figure to watch. (changed: the design's 1M for 1,300 lines)

**The order.** Build and test on a copy of the record. Number at one commit, with the history rebuilt and `title_of` changed in it. Then the chunks run through `apply`. The skill text follows at the skill writer's step. (as designed, the rebuild moved into the numbering commit)

**Not built.** Ways 2 to 5; a stored index or typed links; anchors to report lines; a refusal by size; links beyond one level; a second tool for the coordinator (as designed). And: a frozen history, `trace:`, `history-find:`, `--outside`, the refresh of pointer words, the `title was` field, a YAML form, a `dry-run` flag (a writer applies in its own worktree and hands over the file). (changed)

## 4. Tonight's run through it

- The chunks are the sections, 20 to 32 entries each. FACTS: "The checker and the one library" in three (63 entries); "Landed semantics" (32); "Execution model" with "The harness and the gate" (41, in two if the writer's context asks); the arrays, the specification, the map and the ledger (32). "The container" waits for the `cloud-container` step, as the outline's 3.2.5 says. POSITIONS: "The goal", "History he knows", "The standard and the sources" and "The specification's revision" (23); "The one library and the compiled checker" (26); "Numbers" and "Arrays and the model program" with the three staying entries of "How we work" (26). Nine chunks. The evicted entries are not rewritten; they leave whole to the history at the skill's step, with `remove --note` naming the home.
- The Sonnet scout of a chunk writes one file, at most 1,500 characters per entry: the number and title; for each report section the entry cites, whether `--check 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` resolves it, and its opening line; the commit that established the entry and the last that changed it (`git log --format='%h %ad %s' -S'<title words>' -- FACTS.md`); the status word of each ledger row named; the line of the latest earlier text under the same title in the old history (`git show HASH:FILE`) and its size; the entries that point to it (`F-n+`); for POSITIONS, his dated words on the entry from the old history's dated lines and the `CLIMB-BATCH-*` notes, each at most 300 characters with its date and time.
- The Opus writer of a chunk reads the entry definition, the chunk's entries and the scout's file. It writes the apply file: each entry's new line in the register, with its pointers by number, its merges and its removals; under each, its provenance line with `from` the sections that keep what it cut, `commit` the establishing commit, and a note saying why. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree, reads the sizes, and hands the apply file to the coordinator with a short note: the points for the checker and each entry over 600 with the decision that needs it. The coordinator applies the file on `main`, runs `check --base`, commits the two files and pushes. Chunks apply one after another; the placeholders get their numbers there.
- The pilot: the checker's second chunk and POSITIONS's "The one library and the compiled checker", which hold the kit's FACTS 53, 55 and 58 and POSITIONS 48 and 60. Then the record test as its README says, with one change: one reader on the pilot copy only, and the grader against `key.md`. The pass mark is the first run's totals (27 of 30 for either copy, `grades.md`, "3. Totals") with no scenario below the new entries' first-run score. The scenarios whose entries the pilot did not rewrite read the same text and are the control. A loss is repaired entry by entry, as his 10:14 rule says, and the pilot runs again on those entries before the rest.
- Tokens written, an estimate: nine scouts at about 0.15M, 1.4M; nine writers at about 0.35M, 3.2M; the coordinator's applies, checks and commits, 0.3M; the test, one reader and a grader, about 1.0M. About 6M for the run, beside the builder's 0.8M. The last estimate of this kind ran 56 percent over.

## 5. Decisions for the morning

1. The history is rebuilt: the old texts leave the files, git keeps them at the commit the header names, and the sentence of "The record's form" (`POSITIONS.md:130`) that says the history holds every earlier text is rewritten to say it holds the provenance and the earlier lines from the numbering on. Default: yes, by his 17:01.
2. Each change's block keeps the earlier line, which the tool copies, against provenance only with git for the text. Default: keep the line; it costs disk only, and `check --base` and the record test then need no git.
3. The first numbers are the entries' lines at the base, with gaps, against 1 to N. Default: the lines; they keep the draft's, the outline's and the kit's names.
4. A pointer is the number alone, the words beside it free and unchecked, against the design's number with title words the tool keeps true. Default: the number alone; it removes the one cross-entry rewrite from the tool and is the ledger's way.
5. The former titles are kept, one line per entry, so that a dated note's citation by title resolves after a retitle. Default: keep; it costs 70K bytes once and no writer's time.
6. The history's form is the ledger's Markdown block with one provenance line, not YAML. Default: the block.
7. No "Built:" list in a POSITIONS entry; `P-48+` lists the entries that build it. Default: none.
8. The pilot is two chunks and a one-reader record test with the first run as the baseline, against the kit's two-copy blind run. Default: one reader; the first run's grades are the other arm.

# How the most duplicated conduct rules originated and spread: the evidence

Gathered 2026-10-12. Evidence only: every claim names its commit or its transcript line. A reading is marked as a reading. The rules and their places are the ones of `coordinator-shape.md` section 4.1, at `fb1aa7c7b`.

## 0. How to read this

**Sources.**
- Git: `git log -S'<phrase>'` over the tree for each phrase, per file, to find the commit that first wrote a rule in a place and each later commit that changed its wording there; the commit messages; `git show` for the diffs. Dates are the commits' author dates, UTC.
- Transcripts. **S1** is the first coordinating session, on the branch `transcripts`: `projects/-home-user-fortress/bdff267d-67dc-5bb9-b970-8c3dfaa634b6.jsonl.parts/NNN.jsonl`. **S2** is the current coordinating session, on the branch `transcripts-blinded`: `projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d.until-2026-10-08T15-41.jsonl.parts/NNN.jsonl`; for the records after 2026-10-08T15:41 "S2 now" is the session's own file (the same lines are the top-level file on `transcripts-blinded`). A citation reads "S2 p001 L11119, 2026-09-27T01:18:50Z": the part, the line of the JSONL file, the record's timestamp. Workers' transcripts are the `subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl` files beside them. A line that is a tool call and not a text record is marked so (the briefs to workers are Agent calls; S2 p003 L2730 is the brief of the coordinator skill's writer).
- The curator's messages are the `user` records and the queued messages. He dictates; the speech-to-text slips are left as they are. A queued message is stamped when he sent it and the `user` record when the session took it, so the two can differ by minutes; the `user` record's time is given.

**Models.** Named by tier and version, read from the `model` field of the assistant records of the main thread (or of the worker's own transcript where it is at hand). The coordinating session ran on Fable 5 from the start (2026-08-18T21:03) to 2026-09-08T16:08; on Fable 5.1 from 2026-09-08T16:15 to 2026-09-25T22:48, except two spells on Opus 5 (S1 2026-09-17T11:51 to the end of its backup at 20:31, and S2 2026-09-18T09:50 to 18:16); on Opus 5.5 from 2026-09-25T22:58 to 2026-10-11T06:47 (with 51 Fable 5.1 records on 2026-10-02 10:00 to 10:12); on Fable 5.1 again from 2026-10-11T06:50. Every copy below was written while the model named for it was the coordinating one; where a worker wrote or drafted the text, the worker is named with its model.

**The classes of trigger.** For each copy the event just before it is classed so:
- *failure*: the coordinator broke the rule (or the thing it covers) and he, or the coordinator itself, said so shortly before the copy was written;
- *request*: he asked for this record, rule or rewrite, with no failure of that rule just before;
- *move*: the text was carried into the place by a rewrite, consolidation, split or skill extraction, set going by a request about the whole file or skill, not about the rule;
- *none found*.
A copy that has a failure and a request together is classed by the event the coordinator itself named. Which class a copy belongs to is my reading of the quotes; the quotes are given so that it can be re-read.

**What counts as a copy.** The commit that wrote the rule in one of the places counted in section 4.1, or that rewrote it there in a way that changed its words. A commit that only moved the line, or changed other words of the same line, is not counted.

**Limits.** The searches for failures are regular expressions over the curator's messages and the coordinator's text ("again", "already decided", "I told you", "clock", "guess", "delegate", "yesterday" and the like), read in context; a failure he did not name in such words may be missing. The line numbers are JSONL lines, not paragraph numbers.

## 1. A closed decision is not re-asked; search POSITIONS first (8 places)

**The places at `fb1aa7c7b`.** `protocol.md`:118-120; `README.md`:37; `POSITIONS.md`:1; `POSITIONS.md`:37; `coordinator` SKILL.md:14; decisions.md:38; boot.md:31-32; roles-and-records.md:20.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""skills-lint.py [FILE...]: find the coordinator's agenda in the project skills.

The patterns and their scopes are the "Lint pattern list" of
explorations/reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md:

  fortress-repo and cloud-container, SKILL.md and parts: every set but sources;
  coordinator, SKILL.md and parts: handles (coordinator form), status, stale;
  every references/sources.md: the sources set only.

A file's skill is the folder after "skills/" in its path, so a copy made with
`git show REV:.claude/skills/...` into a folder of the same layout is linted
as the file it copies. A skill not named above takes every set.

With no FILE, every file under the repository's .claude/skills/. Prints
`path:line: set: text` for each hit, the text clipped around the match, and
exits 1 if there is any. Patterns are case-insensitive unless they say (?-i:...).
ALLOW lists hits read and passed, by file, set and a substring of the line.
"""
import os, re, sys

HANDLES = [
    r"\bQ\d+(\.\d+)?\b",
    r"\bitems? (1\d|[2-9]\d|\d{3})[a-z]?\b",
    r"\b(climb )?batch(es)? \d+('s)?\b",
    r"\brung (?!-)[A-Z]\b|\brung's\b",
    r"\b(review|gather|coldread|delta-unfolded|review-routed|judge-review)\.\d+\b",
]
HANDLES_COORDINATOR = HANDLES[:3] + [r"\brung (?!-)[A-Z]\b"]
STATUS = [
